slides.title: Where are we?
slides.text: Where are we? The topics: Attack surfaces so far... Introduction (in May): Warfare, with an indistinct enemy. Social Engineering (in May): Examples - phishing, vishing, tricking. Human weaknesses. System Complexity: Fight back with design principles, standards and formal methods. Crypto 1: Traditional systems - substitution and permutation. (Pre 1976). Crypto 2: (Post 1976) Asymmetric systems: OWF, computational complexity, hashes. IP Networks: Layered structure designed for resilience, not security. Hardening the Internet. OtherNets: Other communication worlds that largely rely on security-by-obscurity. Web Applications: Today we will look at some weaknesses of applications that sit on the Internet - forms of attacks, and their defenses. We will look at injections (particularly SQLi), XSS, CSRF, and pen-testing.

slides.title: Accessing an embedded system
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: Accessing an embedded system DCS true Injection #1: The page allows a command injection into the system The actual command to mount the remote file system for the camera will be: smbmount //192.168.0.5/toto /mnt -o username=toto,password=PASS The trick here is to replace the password PASS with something like “PASS;/bin/command”. After mounting the drive, your command will be executed (it can be anything, but should be something to get you extra access).

slides.title: Bash variables
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: Bash variables ...are called "environment" variables... And we have lots of them ($PATH, $SHELL etc). Sometimes we use them as function definitions: hugh$ env foo='() { echo "Inside" ; };' bash -c "echo Hello" Hello hugh$ env foo='() { echo "Inside" ; }; echo "###"' bash -c "echo Hello" ### Hello hugh$ Note that the extra code after the end of the function definition got executed. It was done when bash started up, and processed the environment variable foo. Injection #2: Running code without calling it... Unfortunately, lots of things on UNIX and MAC systems use bash. People have identified ways of attacking the openSSH login, CGI scripts on web servers, DHCP... I'm shellshocked! ss effectsof shellshock Better get bash fixed ASAP methinks.

slides.title: A web application injection...
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: A web application injection... sqlinjection It is common to link pages to database servers In this scenario, the web server queries a local database server based on a client query. In the example, the client wants to look for records associated with the userName string “hugh”.

slides.title: The system architecture seems innocuous, but... (SQLi) [ i8 ]
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: The system architecture seems innocuous, but... (SQLi) [ i8 ] You access a remote web site, and fill in a form asking for particular information from a database. For example - getting information on a particular user, or a particular product. new request a quote form sql injection Unfortunately, sometimes it is possible to craft a substring containing SQL commands that can do different things from what the developer of the web site intended. As a result... Technique of crafting special substrings with SQL commands is called the “SQL injection attack”.

slides.title: The result is BAD...
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: The result is BAD... sqlinjection We end up with this: The attacker makes up a userName string which has extra stuff in it. This extra stuff may do something malicious when it gets to the database server.

slides.title: Detail on the injection...
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: Detail on the injection... userName web form input is given to a SQL command SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + userName + "'; If the user types in (say) hugh, then you get SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'hugh'; A malicious user could type in (say) a';DROP TABLE users;SELECT * FROM info WHERE 't' = 't And then you get: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'a'; DROP TABLE users; SELECT * FROM info WHERE 't' = 't'; Please dont do this! It is aggressive and nasty.

slides.title: NUS attacks
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: NUS attacks nussec News in 2012... Firstly - it was not NUS, but a departmental web server at NUS that was hacked. The hackers got irritated by a message on the web site, and made it a mission to hack it. The attack was a SQL injection attack, which allowed them to download usercode/password hash entries stored in the SQL database attached to the web server.

slides.title: PHP: control over inputs
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: PHP: control over inputs PHP: Injection from GET input PHP/HTML Code for a web page, for accessing SQL database: <html> <body> ... <?php $matric = $_GET["matric"]; $sql = "SELECT `marks` FROM `test`.`mrks` WHERE userName='$matric'"; $result = mysql_query($sql) or die('Error: ' . mysql_error()); ?> ... <form action="grades.php?method=1" action="get"> Student ID: <input type="text" name="matric"/> <input type="hidden" value=1 name="method"/> <input type="submit"/> </form> </body> </html>

slides.title: PHP: control over inputs
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: PHP: control over inputs Technique 1:mysql_{}real_{}escape_{}string() ... puts backslashes before critical characters: <?php $matric = mysql_real_escape_string($_GET["matric"]); $sql = "SELECT `marks` FROM `test`.`mrks` WHERE userName='$matric'"; $result = mysql_query($sql) or die('Error: ' . mysql_error()); ?> ...which turns.. A' OR '1' = '1 into A' OR '1' = '1 (with the quotes escaped)

slides.title: PHP: control over inputs
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: PHP: control over inputs Technique 2: filters <?php filter_var($somevar, FILTER_SANITIZE_NUMBER_FLOAT, FILTER_FLAG_ALLOW_FRACTION); ... ?> Technique 3: Typing settype($pid, 'integer'); $pid = $_GET["productid"]; $sql = "SELECT * FROM prods WHERE id='$pid'"; Technique 4: hashing $sql = "SELECT * FROM prods WHERE MD5(id)=”.md5($pid);

slides.title: Java: control over inputs
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: Java: control over inputs Java: Injection from getParameter() Java Code in a web page for accessing SQL database: String Matric = request.getParameter("matric"); ... String sel = "SELECT marks FROM test.mrks WHERE userName= '" + Matric + "'"; Statement stmnt = connection.createStatement (); ResultSet resultSet = stmnt.executeQuery(sel); ... We can use similar ideas from the PHP ones: Use Java methods to sanitize input (like mysql_real_escape_string()). Java also has a PreparedStatement class (instead of the Statement class above). Parameters passed in have TYPE (i.e. integer, float..). A PreparedStatement does not automatically stop SQL injections, but it allows you to control the constructed SQL strings more precisely. You may still need to filter the parameters (if for example the parameter was a string).

slides.title: Too many privileges? Also a problem...
slides.section: Attacking web apps: server trusts browser
slides.text: Too many privileges? Also a problem... Base scenario - as before - a web server with SQL access: PHP code in a web page for accessing SQL database: $con = mysql_connect('...','root','rootpasswd') ... Instead should be: $con = mysql_connect('...','nobody','nobodypasswd') ... Why? Consider the situation where someone succeeds with an injection, or with XSS attack, or with some combination. In the two cases: With root access, the attacker could cause significant damage to the database - perhaps removing the database entirely (using the SQL “DROP TABLE” command). Without root access, i.e. only enough access to perform the required task, a successful attacker is limited in the damage that could be done. Note that the nobody user might only be allowed to read and write entries, not create new ones, or delete ones, or delete tables, and so on.

slides.title: Control over outputs [ X ]
slides.section: Attacking web apps: browser trusts server
slides.text: Control over outputs [ X ] Why is it needed? In short, persistent XSS Consider the situation where someone has uploaded some HTML. You may want to display this HTML with rich text (i.e. formatting). However, they may have included some malicious (javascript or other) code in their HTML. Your task then is to take the HTML provided, and output HTML without extra stuff. You are to sanitize the HTML. To do this effectively, there are no real shortcuts: it is best to use a library intended for this purpose. For PHP for example at [X] above. Turn badhtml into goodhtml! <?php require_once '/path/to/library/HTMLPurifier.auto.php'; require_once '/path/to/library/HTMLPurifier.func.php'; $goodhtml = HTMLPurifier($badhtml); ... ... print out $goodhtml... ?>

slides.title: What is pentesting?
slides.section: Pen-testing - for fun and profit!
slides.text: What is pentesting? The complexity of modern (distributed) systems is a security weakness Defences should start while the system is being dreamed up - we use secure technologies, secure development techniques, secure integration and deployment. But despite the best laid plans, the systems still must be continually tested, and risk-assessed/monitored. Let us start with Wikipedia’s view: A penetration test, colloquially known as a pentest or ethical hacking, is an authorized simulated cyberattack on a computer system, performed to evaluate the security of the system... The test is performed to identify weaknesses (or vulnerabilities), including the potential for unauthorized parties to gain access to the system's features and data, as well as strengths, enabling a full risk assessment to be completed. Red and blue teams Blue teams are visible, but it may be the case that red pen-testing teams may be deployed - in these cases, no-one in the IT department knows about them!

slides.text: Pen-testing resources [ i1 , i2 , i3 , ctrl-i4 , i5 ] OWASP: Open Worldwide Application Security Project OWASP is an online community originally focused on Web Application Security. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG), is a web app penetration testing guide. It has a lot of useful detail! See the i2 link above. For remediation, the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) provides web developers with a list of requirements for secure development. See the i3 link above. Other resources The ABS, “Penetration Testing Guidelines For the Financial Industry in Singapore” and a white paper on conducting pentests on organizations are also linked above. An interesting document from Rapid7 on lessons-to-be-learnt is .

slides.title: It is needed, and is NOT hacking!
slides.section: Pen-testing - for fun and profit!
slides.text: It is needed, and is NOT hacking! OWASPTop (OWASP) Pen-testing \neq hacking(Pen-testers are your friends) Security hackers are people skilled in IT who use non-standard means (bugs/errors) to break into computer systems and access data which would otherwise be inaccessible to them. By contrast pen-testing is a professional activity where authorized teams, paid for by the target companies, evaluate the security of a precisely scoped-out system. In order to do this, they may very well use hacking. In the end they help you remediate issues.

slides.title: Who needs pen-testing?
slides.section: Pen-testing - for fun and profit!
slides.text: Who needs pen-testing? Top Mostly accurate answer? Any business... From MAS, “Technology Risk Management Guidelines”, we have guidance for Financial Institutions: 9.4.1 Vulnerability assessment (VA) is the process of identifying, assessing and discovering security vulnerabilities in a system. The FI should conduct VAs regularly... 9.4.4 The FI should carry out penetration tests in order to conduct an in-depth evaluation of the security posture of the system through simulations of actual attacks on the system. The FI should conduct penetration tests on internet-facing systems at least annually.

slides.title: Pen-testers follow these steps
slides.section: Pen-testing - for fun and profit!
slides.text: Pen-testers follow these steps Pen Testing Satges Extra steps than “hacking” and a different focus Pen-testers discuss the scope with the client first, and also report back on what they found, and best practices for remediation. In a recent pen-test project here at SoC, only about 25% of the time spent was direct hacking activities.

slides.text: Pen-tester pre-engagement [ X , ctrl-i6 ] Scope and contracts... Scoping for a test might include a scoping survey, and meetings: For example see [X] above. Nondisclosure Agreement (NDA): For your client to protect itself. Master Service Agreement (MSA): contains contractual matters between the parties, including a “get out of jail free” card, payment terms... Statement of Work (SoW): Outlines an organization’s project-specific work to be executed by a service provider. This can be part of the MSA. Rules of Engagement (RoE): This specifies guidelines and constraints of a pen-testing execution, and can be part of SoW or as a separate document. For example, see the link at [ctrl-i6] above. slides.title: Summary: Web Applications
slides.section: Pen-testing - for fun and profit!
slides.text: Attacking web apps: server trusts browserAttacking web apps: browser trusts serverPen-testing - for fun and profit! What is it? And... what do they do? Summary: Web Applications Today, we have seen... Servers trusting browsers - We saw a range of injections, where servers placed too much trust in the client (the browser), and as a result, malicious activities happened. We saw command and SQLi (SQL injections), and then how programmatically we can defend the servers, by ensuring that the input from the client/browser was sanitised. Browsers trusting servers - We saw a range of XSS (Cross Site Scripting) attacks, where browsers/clients placed too much trust in the server, and as a result, malicious activities happened. We saw reflected and stored XSS, CSRF and clickjacking, and then how programmatically we can defend the servers, by ensuring that not only the input from the client/browser was sanitised, but also the output from the server. Pen-testing - Organisations should consider hiring a pen-testing company. They use a range of techniques to help remediate security issues in applications.
